items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.

items.title: C60 was discovered while looking for interstellar carbon chains
items.claim: In 1985 Harold Kroto (Sussex), Robert Curl and Richard Smalley (Rice University) were vaporising graphite with a laser to mimic carbon clusters in stellar atmospheres. They saw a strong peak at mass 720 — exactly 60 carbon atoms. They proposed it had the structure of a soccer ball.
items.prompt: Why was C60 such a surprise?

options.text: Carbon was previously thought not to form clusters
Carbon's only known pure allotropes were diamond and graphite; no one had proposed a molecular form of carbon, and a hollow spherical cage of 60 atoms was structurally unprecedented
It was made of an unknown isotope

items.reveal_title: A soccer ball in a vacuum chamber
items.reveal:
C60 has the structure of a truncated icosahedron — 60 carbons at the vertices of a soccer-ball pattern, with 12 pentagonal and 20 hexagonal faces. Every carbon is sp2 hybridised and bonds to three neighbours.

Kroto, Curl and Smalley named it 'buckminsterfullerene' after Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes inspired the structure. They won the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Fullerenes opened up a third class of carbon allotropes. Carbon nanotubes (rolled-up sheets) were identified in 1991. Graphene (a single layer) was isolated by Geim and Novoselov in 2004 — they won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

C60 has since been detected in interstellar clouds (2010), solving an 85-year-old mystery about a 'diffuse interstellar band' in stellar spectra.
items.why: A whole new class of carbon allotropes appeared in a high-vacuum laser experiment. Discoveries can land where you weren't looking.
